view.text:
11:47 PM. The storm has been working at the windows for an hour.

Across the hall, 6D is dark. It has been dark most nights since March. Since the night Teo knocked on your door at two in the morning, and you stood on this side of it and didn't answer. The police came later. You never asked him why.

Someone knocks. Three times, evenly, the way people knock when they already know you're home.

Through the peephole: a woman in a dark coat, soaked through, hair flat against her face. She isn't shivering. She is looking straight into the lens, as if she can see you on the other side of it.

"Please," she says. "You already let me in."

You have never seen her before. Your hand is on the deadbolt. In your pocket, your thumb finds the guitar pick. You've never been able to get rid of it.

You open the door. She steps past you before you have decided to step aside, and the cold comes in with her.

"Thank you," she says. "Again."

You opened it this time. The relief lasts less than a second.

Up close she is younger than you thought, and older. Water runs off her coat and pools around her shoes and doesn't spread. In her hand is a brass key on a paper tag. The tag says BASEMENT 07 in faded marker.

"Mara," she says, as though you have asked her that many times. She sits at your table without taking off the coat.

"I need to go down to 07," she says. "And I need someone to see what's in it. Someone who'll tell Teo he wasn't imagining things." She turns the key over and over. "He's never opened his door for me. Not once."

A pause.

"That isn't true. He did tonight. Not here. Somewhere else."

The lights go out at 11:58. Mara doesn't react. In the dark you can hear the water leaving her coat, steady as a clock.

"There are nights people try to forget," she says. "That doesn't mean nobody is still inside them."

The key stops turning.

"Look at the tag."

view.text:
Mara stands. "I can show you what's in 07. After that, you decide what deserves to stay."

Across the hall, Teo's chain lifts.

"Don't go down with her," he says through the gap. "Go up. Up is just weather."

Mara looks at his door for a long moment. "He's never trusted a door in his life," she says. "Neither have you."

She goes first. Six flights, and her hand never touches the rail. The basement is dry, which is wrong; the storm is everywhere else.

Storage cages in rows, numbered in stencil. Unit 07 at the far end, padlocked. Mara holds out the key, but not toward the lock. Toward you.

"You do it," she says. "It has to be someone who's still deciding."

The key turns in the cage door's lock without a sound. The door still doesn't move.

Below the keyhole hangs a second lock you have never seen on anything in this building: a padlock with four brass dials, green at the edges.

Mara holds the paper tag up between you, so the storm light from the high window falls on it. On the digits that weren't there an hour ago.

"Go on," she says.

The dials are cold and stiff. 1019.

The shackle drops open with a sound like a held breath let go.

Inside 07 there is a folding chair, facing the door. On the seat lies a guitar pick. Yours: the same chipped edge, the same pale scuff. But old, and dry, as if it has been waiting here a long time. The scratches have worn nearly away.

Mara doesn't go in. "That's what's left of the night you answered him," she says.

view.text:
Three knocks. Behind you. At the end of the row of cages, where the stairs should be, there is a door.

The same paint as yours. The same brass peephole. The same scratch beside the lock.

Your door.

You put your eye to the peephole.

Someone is standing on the other side, soaked through. Your coat. Your hands. Your face.

For a second you think it's a mirror.

Then the person blinks.

You didn't.

view.text:
"I know what you chose," they say. It's your voice, from the wrong side of the wood.

"I kept it locked. I sat against the door and listened to everything."

Beside you, Mara has gone very still. She isn't looking at the door. She's looking at you. This is what she needed someone to see.

"Teo opened his door for her. I heard the chain. He never opens it for anyone."

They try the handle. It doesn't move. They put a palm flat against the door. You can hear them breathing. Exactly as you are.

"I did what we always do. I kept it shut. You're the one who changed."

"Why do you get to be the real one?"

They're waiting.

Lock it, and the other you is gone. You won't have to hear them again.

Open it, and they come in. Neither of you knows what happens when two versions of one life meet.

changed: The brass key is in Mara's hand, beside you. And it is in your hand. You can feel both, like holding one thing in two hands.
Your guitar pick is in your hand. It always was.
Mara is beside you. She looks relieved, and very tired, like someone who has been holding a door shut for a long time.

view.text:
You turn the deadbolt. It is loud, louder than it should be.

Through the peephole, the other you goes still. You know that expression. It's the face you make when you know no one is coming.

"1019" fades from the key's paper tag, and "MARA" from the guitar pick, like breath off a mirror, and then there is nothing left to read.

When you look up, Mara is gone. Where she stood, the floor is dry.

Behind you, the folding chair in 07 still faces the door. Mara wanted someone to see. You saw. You locked it anyway.

At 12:30 every light in the building comes back at once. Somewhere below, a fridge begins to hum as if nothing happened.

Then, three knocks. Slow. Patient.

You don't move until they stop.

Somewhere, you made a different choice.
